item.title: Why neutrinos matter as Francis Halzen wins 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics?
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07
STOCKHOLM, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- Buried deep beneath the Antarctic ice, thousands of light sensors wait for flashes left by neutrinos, elusive particles that can travel across the universe almost undisturbed. By turning a cubic kilometre of South Pole ice into a giant detector, physicist Francis Halzen helped open a new window on the cosmos. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded Halzen the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics on Tuesday "for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin." WHAT ARE NEUTRINOS, AND WHY DO THEY MATTER? Neutrinos are among the smallest known particles. They carry no electric charge, have extremely little mass, and interact so weakly with matter that most pass straight through the Earth without leaving a trace. Olle Eriksson, a member of the Nobel Committee for Physics and professor at Uppsala University, told Xinhua that detecting neutrinos is extremely challenging: "Through my thumbnail, there are 65 billion neutrinos that go through every second, and I don't feel it." But once detected, they can reveal information about events occurring far out in the universe. Scientists have long known that the cosmos contains natural particle accelerators capable of producing particles with energies far beyond those achievable in laboratories on Earth. The origins of the highest-energy cosmic particles, however, have remained difficult to trace. Cosmic rays carry electric charge and are deflected by magnetic fields as they travel through space. Neutrinos, unlike other particles, are electrically neutral and travel essentially in a straight line, allowing scientists to trace their direction back toward the violent environments where they were produced. HOW DID HALZEN TURN SOUTH POLE ICE INTO A TELESCOPE? In 1988, Halzen, the Belgian-born scientist, presented the idea of installing light sensors deep in Antarctic ice. When one of the rare neutrinos collides with an atomic nucleus, it can produce a charged particle that generates a faint flash of blue light as it moves through the transparent ice. Sensors can capture that light and help scientists reconstruct where the neutrino came from. The idea eventually became IceCube, a detector using an entire cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice. Completed in 2011, it contains 5,160 light sensors, mostly between about 1,450 and 2,450 metres below the surface. The depth matters. "There, the ice is very clear, no air bubbles, no dirt, no dust," said Eriksson, adding that this condition allows faint flashes to travel hundreds of metres before being absorbed. The effort paid off. In 2013, IceCube researchers reported the first strong evidence for high-energy neutrinos arriving from distant space. With more data, they were able to establish that some of the particles originated far outside the solar system. Eriksson said the achievement helps humanity better understand its surroundings and its place in the universe by providing information about extreme cosmic events that cannot easily be obtained in other ways. The immediate significance lies mainly in expanding fundamental knowledge, he said, adding that major scientific discoveries can also lead to practical applications that were impossible to foresee when the research began. WHY HALZEN, AND WHAT COMES NEXT? IceCube is the work of a large international collaboration involving hundreds of scientists and engineers. "Even though it is a large collaboration, we could still identify one person who was the pivotal, most important contributor to that experimental buildup and the experimental discovery," said Eriksson. "It was a long journey, but ... it finally worked," Halzen recalled the early phases at Tuesday's Nobel press conference, describing how the success was not guaranteed nearly 40 years ago but made possible by critical contributions from many people. The journey is continuing. Scientists are planning IceCube-Gen2, which is expected to expand the instrumented volume at the South Pole to about eight cubic kilometres, while other neutrino observatories are being developed around the world. Halzen said opening a new window on the universe often leads to unexpected discoveries. For neutrino astronomy, that window may only have begun to open. ■

item.title: Feature: At 16, Sun shines in her WTA 1000 debut at China Open
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-06
China's 16-year-old Sun Xinran made a memorable WTA 1000 debut at the China Open, advancing to the third round after beating two higher-ranked opponents before losing to world No. 4 Coco Gauff. The US Open girls singles champion said the experience boosted her confidence and gave her valuable lessons as she steps into the professional game. by sportswriters Li Chunyu and Wang Chunyan BEIJING, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- China's 16-year-old Sun Xinran stepped into the spotlight at the China Open, showing maturity beyond her years in her WTA 1000 debut. The girls' singles champion at this year's US Open and runner-up at both the French Open and Wimbledon, Sun advanced through the first two rounds in Beijing before her campaign ended with a 7-5, 6-1 loss to world No. 4 Coco Gauff of the United States on Monday. Sun had previously beaten Germany's Eva Lys and 27th seed Cristina Bucsa of Spain, going further than many expected in her first China Open appearance. "There were chances I could take, but there was some collapse in the second set," the teenager reflected after the match against Gauff. "Her rhythm is much faster than other players. She's able to mix it up and serves more powerful, much better than me. There are so many things I can learn from her." Playing at the China Open for the first time, the Shenzhen native admitted she had been nervous but also proud to compete on Diamond Court during China's National Day holiday. "I'm just so happy to play on that court. This is China, my home country. The crowd supported me a lot. I can hear them. They gave me energy," the wildcard player said. Sun frequently clenched her fist after winning points, feeding off the support from the stands as she tested herself against higher-ranked opponents. "This tournament gave me opportunity to play against top players. From the first round to the third round, my opponents are getting higher in their rankings. It just shows I have the ability to play against them. This really motivates me to improve myself." Competing in a WTA 1000 main draw also required Sun to adjust to a level of intensity beyond the junior circuit, but her aggressive returning and composure off the court offered signs that she was becoming more comfortable at senior level. "I just started playing professional matches. I don't want to give myself so big pressure. I want to focus on my tennis, move forward step by step, and we will see what is going to happen," she said. Describing herself as an "all-round player," Sun said years of training and competition had given her confidence in her preparation. "I've played many matches with great coaches and facilities. Our team has been working hard towards our goals," Sun said. "I have my interpretation of each game. I make full preparation before matches and focus on implementing the plan. I take my own pace." This year has marked a breakthrough for Sun, who reached the girls' singles final at three Grand Slam tournaments. "It gave me so many experience to play on the big court and also play with very good opponents. I think that really helps me to improve myself and play better in the profession," said Sun. "Tennis is not only about the strategies and tactics in competitions. Off the court, it is also important to understand how to warm up and how to recover after matches," the teenager added. Olympic champion Zheng Qinwen also offered encouragement to Sun during the China Open, saying, "She has achieved a lot as a teenager. I didn't manage to pull off what she has done when I was a junior, so I think she's incredible." "I told her [Zheng] she is my idol. She had great milestones in her career, such as the Paris Olympics and the Australian Open," Sun noted. "I'm still a junior player. I will continue to learn from her. I will try to improve my serve and my energy on the court." ■

item.title: Brewing new trails, Yunnan coffee carries Chinese aroma across Asia-Pacific
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-06
* Yunnan sits on the northern fringe of the global coffee-growing "bean belt," the equatorial zone between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn. For centuries, its rolling highlands were known as China's tea heartland. Over the past two decades, steady investment, improved farming techniques and booming domestic consumption have nurtured a thriving home-grown coffee industry. * Cross-border innovation in coffee culture is also taking shape across the Lancang-Mekong basin, which China shares with Myanmar, Laos, Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam. * While Southeast Asia remains at the heart of Yunnan's Asia-Pacific coffee trade, the beans are travelling much farther -- all the way to New Zealand, where they remain a niche but notable newcomer to the specialty-coffee scene. KUALA LUMPUR, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- When Thomas Ooi first tasted Yunnan coffee in Beijing in 2015, its savory, almost beef-jerky-like character struck him as unusual. Back then, few in Malaysia's coffee scene had their eye on beans from Yunnan, a Chinese province better known for tea. A decade later, everything has changed. Ooi, founder of Ghostbird Coffee Roastery in Kuala Lumpur, imported his first batch of Yunnan specialty beans in 2025, put them on his cafe menu, and watched them sell out in just two months. The growing popularity reflects a broader regional shift, as coffee from China's mountainous southwest gains ground beyond its home market, finding new drinkers across the Asia-Pacific and opening fresh avenues for trade, cultural exchange and appreciation of taste. EMERGING COFFEE ORIGIN Yunnan sits on the northern fringe of the global coffee-growing "bean belt," the equatorial zone between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn. For centuries, its rolling highlands were known as China's tea heartland. Over the past two decades, steady investment, improved farming techniques and booming domestic consumption have nurtured a thriving home-grown coffee industry. Yunnan's coffee industry spans six core growing zones: Pu'er, Baoshan, Lincang, Dehong, Xishuangbanna and Nujiang, each boasting unique strengths in nurturing specialty coffee. In the first eight months of 2026, the province exported 11,000 tonnes of coffee with a total value of 450 million yuan (67 million U.S. dollars). "I think Yunnan is very interesting, not just because of the coffee varietals themselves. I think the producers from Yunnan are very innovative," Ooi said, sharing his plan to visit Yunnan's coffee farms at the end of this year's harvest season, which will bring along fellow roaster friends eager to see the plantations firsthand. Malaysia is among Yunnan's key Asian export destinations. According to the provincial international trade association, Yunnan coffee was exported to 43 countries and regions in 2025, with European and Asian countries being leading destinations for Yunnan's coffee shipments. Within Asia, Vietnam and Malaysia stand as the two major markets. CROSS-BORDER BLENDS For Hanoi coffee specialist Pham Duy Anh, Yunnan beans are steadily winning over Vietnamese consumers, with an increasing number of specialty cafes and roasters now offering them. He said their appeal lies in improving quality with each harvest and a range of processing methods that suit Vietnamese drinkers seeking new flavors. "Diverse processing methods like washed, natural, honey and anaerobic have kept the beans from being boxed into a single flavor profile, giving drinkers notes such as mild wine, raisin, guava, tea and watermelon," Anh said, depicting it as an advantage in a market that values diversity and personalization in the coffee experience. Trade ties between Yunnan and Vietnam have grown beyond simple commodity exchanges, creating an environment that has helped fuel the growing coffee trade between the two sides. Joint initiatives, including the China-Vietnam coffee festival, industry-led trade alliances, enterprise matchmaking and supply-chain field visits, have built deep industry-to-industry connections. At the Fourth China International Supply Chain Expo in Beijing in June, a 40-square-meter Yunnan-Vietnam-themed coffee booth drew wide attention by highlighting its edge in frontier-based cross-border coffee supply chains. Cross-border innovation in coffee culture is also taking shape across the Lancang-Mekong basin, which China shares with Myanmar, Laos, Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam. Omar Ali, co-founder and general manager of SinoTaste, created "Mekong Coffee with Six Flavors," a multi-country blended coffee drawing beans from all six Lancang-Mekong nations, after sampling roughly 50 bean lots and testing dozens of formulas. "When you make a multi-origin blend, the point is not to make one origin stand out. It is about how these coffees complement each other and create something none could achieve on its own," Omar Ali said. "It mirrors partnerships: every country and culture carries distinct strengths; brought together, they produce new possibilities." TO GO FURTHER AFIELD While Southeast Asia remains at the heart of Yunnan's Asia-Pacific coffee trade, the beans are travelling much farther -- all the way to New Zealand, where they remain a niche but notable newcomer to the specialty-coffee scene. New Zealand's cafe culture has relied heavily on beans from established Latin American producers such as Brazil and Colombia. But Yunnan green beans have begun appearing at a handful of local roasteries, Radio New Zealand reported. MQ Coffee, based in Auckland, New Zealand's largest city, is among the businesses giving Yunnan coffee a foothold in New Zealand. Its co-owner, Wang Yanqi, said the beans have improved markedly in quality in recent years, just as international interest in China as a source of coffee has begun to grow. The company features Yunnan beans in its training and tasting sessions, putting them side by side with coffees from other origins to give participants a firsthand taste of Yunnan's distinctive flavor profiles. Wang noted that some Yunnan coffees have good sweetness and body, allowing their distinctive coffee character to shine through even with milk added. The company has organized study tours for New Zealand coffee professionals and enthusiasts to visit growing regions inside Yunnan, where they could gain direct insight into local coffee farming and processing practices. To turn overseas interest into repeat purchases, Yunnan coffee must become more competitive on quality, price and reliability of supply, Wang said. The quality of Yunnan coffee has improved significantly over the past decade, Ooi said. "Now we are learning about its taste profiles, but we want to understand them more deeply." (Video reporters: Li Shutong, Wang Jiawei, Zul and Jonathan Tham Yao Ming; Video editors: Zhao Tianlin, Liu Xiaorui, Zhang Yuhong and Zhang Yichi)■

item.title: China urges France, Germany to uphold open cooperation, free trade
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-06
BEIJING, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- China hopes that France and Germany will uphold open cooperation and free trade, observe World Trade Organization rules, and refrain from encouraging the European Union (EU) to use protectionist tools at every turn, a spokesperson for the Ministry of Commerce said on Tuesday. When asked to comment on media reports that France and Germany had urged the EU to make greater use of trade defense measures and roll out a number of new protectionist tools, the spokesperson said China has always maintained that interdependence is not a risk, intertwined interests do not pose a threat, and open cooperation represents the right path to development. Protectionism cannot enhance competitiveness, and decoupling and cutting off supply chains will only harm others without benefiting oneself, the spokesperson said. As major economies, France and Germany should not politicize trade and economic issues or overstretch the concept of national security. They should avoid going down the wrong path in the wrong way, which would ultimately backfire on themselves, the spokesperson added. ■

item.title: China firmly opposes U.S. arms sales to China's Taiwan region: spokesperson
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-06
BEIJING, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- China remains firmly opposed to U.S. arms sales to China's Taiwan region, Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Guo Jiakun said on Tuesday, stressing that the country's position is clear. Guo made the remarks in response to media reports that Taiwan recently received two F-16V fighter jets purchased from the United States and plans to receive another 64 within the year. Guo said the U.S. side needs to implement the important common understandings reached at the meeting between the two countries' presidents, abide by the one-China principle and the three China-U.S. joint communiques, and act prudently on the Taiwan question. "The Taiwan question is China's internal affair, and resolving it is a matter for the Chinese ourselves that brooks no external interference," he said. ■

item.title: New professions show China's industrial, livelihood progress
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-06
BEIJING, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- A stream of new occupations is emerging at the forefront of China's new technologies, industries and business models, mirroring industrial upgrading and improvements in people's livelihoods. In the low-altitude economy sector alone, newly added positions such as drone swarm flight planners, low-altitude logistics specialists, and low-altitude intelligent connected system administrators stand out in the eighth batch of new professions recently released by the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security and other government departments. Occupations tied to the booming digital economy are also reshaping work in China, including AI engineering technicians, intelligent connected vehicle testers, embodied intelligent robot application technicians, and microgrid administrators, among others. The release of 11 new occupations and 23 new job types in the eighth batch marks a fresh update to the country's occupational catalog. Such updates serve as a talent "barometer" reflecting the pulse of China's industrial transformation, industry insiders noted. Take the low-altitude economy for example. The first batch of new occupations, released in 2019, introduced the drone pilots to meet the urgent demand for drone operations. The second batch added drone assembly and maintenance technicians, a role created to close the gap in equipment operation and maintenance for the emerging drone industry. As the drone industry has grown, new positions in the seventh and eighth batches have taken on responsibilities that expand from single technical operations to cross-cutting application fields such as logistics delivery, cultural tourism operations, and urban governance. The continuous release of new occupations reflects China's industrial system moving toward higher-end, smarter and greener development, said Li Qiang, vice president of online job-seeking platform Zhaopin. "Policy support expands and underpins the talent supply, while the job market absorbs in tandem. New occupations are both a precise mapping of the industrial development trends and a positive guide for the talent market," Li said. Beyond industrial upgrading, changes in China's new occupations also reflect evolving demands in people's livelihoods, with new jobs in the modern services sector continuing to expand. Industry insiders noted that as people's quality of life has been improving, producer services have moved toward specialization and the higher end of the value chain, while consumer services have developed toward higher quality, greater diversity, and convenience. The size of China's service sector is expected to expand beyond 100 trillion yuan (about 14.8 trillion U.S. dollars) in the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), according to the National Development and Reform Commission, the country's top economic planner. Industry insiders say the consumer services sector will be explored to unlock economic growth potential, with broad scope for developing residential services, health services, aged care, and childcare. Therefore, progress in this sector is expected to generate even more new jobs. China has been dynamically updating its occupational classification catalog. Since 2019, the country has issued eight batches of 121 new occupations. In 2020, the second batch introduced health-related new professions including healthcare attendants and rehabilitation assistive technology consultants. Subsequent batches continued this momentum, adding niche occupations and job types such as ski patrol rescuers, family education instructors, age-friendly renovation designers, and incense-making artisans. China's State Council has issued a plan to implement the employment-first strategy during the 15th Five-Year Plan period, calling for stronger synergy among macroeconomic policies on employment and highlighting efforts to stabilize employment in labor-intensive industries, expand employment in the service sector, and tap employment potential in emerging fields. "The emergence of new occupations is a direct response to new applications of technologies, fresh market changes, and new consumer demands," said Li Chang'an, a researcher at the Academy of China Open Economy Studies under the University of International Business and Economics. "Every update of the occupational catalog will inject more talent-driven momentum into the country's industrial development in the future alongside the advancement of the occupational standard system, alignment between talent cultivation and supply, and rules and systems to safeguard the progress of the sector," Li added. ■

item.title: Longer trips, richer experiences: China's National Day holiday reveals shifting tourism trends
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05
* Chinese travelers have ventured farther during the National Day holiday, with family trips and experience-oriented travel on the rise. * Former revolutionary base areas have drawn renewed interest from holidaymakers, with visits offering travelers a chance to learn about the country's revolutionary history and reflect on the difficult years that helped shape modern China. * More international travelers are flocking to China to experience the country for themselves, riding a rising wave of global fascination with everything from the scenery and culture to its lifestyles and, more recently, Chinese brands and design. BEIJING, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- Five days into China's week-long National Day holiday, millions are still immersed in the sights, sounds and flavors of the season -- traveling, dining, exploring and enjoying the break. Yet this year, the scenes are subtly different. Travelers have ventured farther as the Mid-Autumn Festival holiday fell just three days before the National Day holiday, while family trips and experience-oriented travel are on the rise, according to travel agencies. "It points to a fundamental shift in the logic of tourism consumption, as travelers focus more on the quality of time and the richness of their experiences," said Bu Xiting, a researcher with the Communication University of China. LONGER BREAKS, RICHER CHOICES Data from Chinese online travel platform Tuniu shows that tours of 10 days or more are particularly popular during this holiday period, accounting for 26 percent of bookings. Yuan You, an internet company employee, spent three days of her 13-day break in Jiuzhaigou, southwest China's Sichuan Province, before heading to the provincial capital Chengdu for woodworking classes. "The holiday is rich while maintaining a relaxed pace," she said. Authorities across the country have rolled out a wide range of activities, consumer vouchers and subsidies to spur holiday spending. Shanghai, for example, has launched about 200 major consumption events, backed by consumer vouchers worth roughly 100 million yuan (around 14.85 million U.S. dollars). The offerings range from watching films and dining to purchasing digital products and cars, encouraging consumers to explore a broader spectrum of spending experiences. Cultural institutions, too, are broadening the ways people can experience and consume culture. The Sichuan Museum extended its holiday hours and launched a themed night tour, while Beijing's Zhongshan Park brought museums, cultural institutions and innovative brands together to create a market street featuring culture-inspired products. As more new energy vehicles hit the roads during the holiday, authorities have taken measures to ensure adequate charging facilities and convenient services. During last year's eight-day Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day holiday period, Chinese travelers made 888 million domestic trips and spent a combined 809 billion yuan, according to the Ministry of Culture and Tourism. This year, data shows that foot traffic and revenue at 78 major shopping streets and commercial districts monitored by the Ministry of Commerce rose 3.4 percent and 5.3 percent year on year, respectively, from Oct. 1 to 3. RED TOURISM, ROBOTS AND RURAL EXPERIENCES As China marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March, former revolutionary base areas have drawn renewed interest from holidaymakers, with visits offering travelers a chance to learn about the country's revolutionary history and reflect on the difficult years that helped shape modern China. In Yan'an, northwest China's Shaanxi Province, a street has staged special activities including performances of songs from the revolutionary years and a large-scale bonfire gathering. Visitor numbers on the first day of the holiday rose about 20 percent year on year. The holiday has also turned some of China's newest robots into part of the consumer experience, putting embodied intelligence to work alongside traditional culture in tourist attractions, shopping districts and ancient towns. At a cultural district in Chengdu, robots performed dances inspired by local opera's face-changing art and used digital technology to recreate tanghua, a traditional form of sugar painting. On Chunxi Road, a humanoid robot has gone beyond entertainment to take on the role of a store manager, greeting customers and recommending products rather than simply performing for them. China's growing network of robot training bases is preparing more machines for roles beyond the factory floor -- and beyond the country's borders. In the first half of 2026, Chinese manufacturers accounted for 97 percent of humanoid robot shipments worldwide, according to a report released at the 2026 World Robot Conference. Years of efforts to restore the environment and revitalize rural areas are also paying off. On a ridge overlooking the Miyun Reservoir in Beijing, visitors can hike to a viewing platform and enjoy outdoor concerts amid the pine trees. With roads, infrastructure and public services extending deeper into the countryside, some once-remote villages are emerging as new destinations for holidaymakers. Caijiagou, a former impoverished hillside village in east China's Shandong Province, has transformed into an art-themed destination, with murals adorning residential walls. Village official Liang Yunhui said the village has repurposed idle rural homes into cultural spaces such as an art gallery and a musical instrument museum, while hosting events featuring traditional crafts, cultural fairs and folk music. "In total, we have received more than 500,000 visits over the years," he said. On travel platform Fliggy, the number of users purchasing travel products featuring natural scenery and villages surged by nearly 50 percent from the same holiday period last year. "More travelers are seeking immersive experiences, from sampling local cuisine and making intangible cultural heritage crafts to watching distinctive performances, allowing them to gain a deeper appreciation of local culture," said a manager with Tuniu. CHINA HAUL While many Chinese tourists are venturing farther around the world, more international travelers are flocking to China to experience the country for themselves, riding a rising wave of global fascination with everything from the scenery and culture to its lifestyles and, more recently, Chinese brands and design. Tennis star Novak Djokovic, in Beijing for the China Open, was seen trying his hand at Chinese calligraphy at the Summer Palace, a former imperial garden. After a match, he used a traditional Chinese seal to put his mark on fans' keepsakes instead of signing autographs. Huaqiangbei, a sprawling electronics marketplace in south China's tech hub Shenzhen, has become a magnet for foreign shoppers looking to experience China's tech scene firsthand. Bryan Lamothe-Arice from the United States was browsing smart devices. "I'm particularly interested in the electric bikes and all kinds of flying devices here. I'm going to tell my friends to come here. There are tech products everywhere." China's border crossings are expected to see about 2.15 million passenger trips a day on average during the National Day holiday, according to the National Immigration Administration. That growing international interest is also showing up in spending. Overseas visitors spent 263.6 billion yuan in China in the first seven months of 2026, up 27.8 percent year on year, according to the commerce ministry.
